section.heading: 2.5. One-Sided Limits and Continuity
One-Sided Limits
section.paragraph: Consider the function $$f$$ defined by
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} {x - 1} & { {if}x < 0} \\ {x + 1} & { {if}x \geq 0} \end{cases}$$

From the graph of $$f$$ shown in Figure 37, we see that the function $$f$$ does not have a limit as $$x$$ approaches zero because, no matter how close $$x$$ is to zero, $$f(x)$$ takes on values that are close to $$1$$ if $$x$$ is positive and values that are close to $$- 1$$ if $$x$$ is negative. Therefore, $$f(x)$$ cannot be close to a single number $$L$$ —no matter how close $$x$$ is to zero. Now, if we restrict $$x$$ to be greater than zero (to the right of zero), then we see that $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to $$1$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to zero. In this situation, we say that the right-hand limit of $$f$$ as $$x$$ approaches zero (from the right) is $$1$$ , written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}f(x) = 1$$

image.alt: Details A closed circle and an open circle are plotted at the coordinate (0, 1) and (0, negative 1) respectively. The line labeled y = f(x), enters the third quadrant, slopes upward, slanting to the right and discontinues at the open point (0, negative 1) and continues at the point (0, 1), slopes upward, slanting to the right in the first quadrant and exits the quadrant at the bottom left of the viewing window.

figure.caption: The function $$f$$ does not have a limit as $$x$$ approaches zero.

section.paragraph: Similarly, we see that $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to $$- 1$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to, but to the left of, zero. In this situation, we say that the left-hand limit of $$f$$ as $$x$$ approaches zero (from the left) is $$- 1$$ , written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}f(x) = - 1$$
These limits are called one-sided limits. More generally, we have the following informal definitions.

note.title: One-Sided Limits
note.heading: One-Sided Limits
note.paragraph: The function $$f$$ has the right-hand limit $$L$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ from the right, written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = L$$
if the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to $$L$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to (but not equal to) $$a$$ and to the right of $$a$$ .
Similarly, the function $$f$$ has the left-hand limit $$M$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ from the left, written
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = M$$
if the values of $$f(x)$$ can be made as close to $$M$$ as we please by taking $$x$$ sufficiently close to (but not equal to) $$a$$ and to the left of $$a$$ .

section.paragraph: The connection between one-sided limits and the two-sided limit defined earlier is given by the following theorem.

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be a function that is defined for all values of $$x$$ close to $$x = a$$ with the possible exception of $$a$$ itself. Then
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$
if and only if
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = L$$

section.paragraph: Thus, the two-sided limit exists if and only if the one-sided limits exist and are equal.

list.item: Show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x)$$ exists by studying the one-sided limits of $$f$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$x = 0$$ .
Show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}g(x)$$ does not exist.

For $$x \leq 0$$ , $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}( - x) = 0$$ and for $$x > 0$$ , we find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\sqrt{x} = 0$$ Thus, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x) = 0$$ (Figure 38a).

We have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}g(x) = - 1$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}g(x) = 1$$ and since these one-sided limits are not equal, we conclude that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}g(x)$$ does not exist (Figure 38b). section.heading: Continuous Functions
section.paragraph: Continuous functions will play an important role throughout most of our study of calculus. Loosely speaking, a function is continuous at a point if the graph of the function at that point is devoid of holes, gaps, jumps, or breaks. Consider, for example, the graph of the function $$f$$ depicted in Figure 39.

image.alt: Details A discontinuous curve is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis has 4 tick marks labeled a, b, c, and d from left to right on the positive x axis with unequal interval. The curve starts in the second quadrant slopes downward to the right and reaches its low point close to the y axis, further slopes upward to the right, crosses the y axis to enter the first quadrant and connects an open point from where a perpendicular is dropped to the x intercept labeled a, the curve continues to slope upward to peak at another open point that is plotted vertically below a point, from which a perpendicular is dropped to the x intercept labeled b. Thereafter the curve slopes downward to the right to reach a point, from which a perpendicular is dropped to the x intercept labeled c. The curve continues at an open point plotted vertically above the point connecting the perpendicular raised from the x intercept labeled c. Further the curve slopes downward to the right and takes an upward bend to form a U shaped curve, which continues to slope close to the perpendicular raised from the x intercept labeled d. The curve continues on the right of the perpendicular raised from the x intercept labeled d, slopes upward, arching to the right and exits the viewing window.

figure.caption: The graph of this function is not continuous at $$x = a$$ , $$x = b$$ , $$x = c$$ , and $$x = d$$ .

section.paragraph: Let’s take a closer look at the behavior of $$f$$ at or near $$x = a$$ , $$x = b$$ , $$x = c$$ , and $$x = d$$ . First, note that $$f$$ is not defined at $$x = a$$ ; that is, $$x = a$$ is not in the domain of $$f$$ , thereby resulting in a “hole” in the graph of $$f$$ . Next, observe that the value of $$f$$ at $$b$$ , $$f(b)$$ , is not equal to the limit of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$b$$ , resulting in a “jump” in the graph of $$f$$ at $$x = b$$ . The function $$f$$ does not have a limit at $$x = c$$ since the left-hand and right-hand limits of $$f(x)$$ are not equal, also resulting in a jump in the graph of $$f$$ at $$x = c$$ . Finally, the limit of $$f$$ does not exist at $$x = d$$ , resulting in a break in the graph of $$f$$ . The function $$f$$ is discontinuous at each of these numbers. It is continuous everywhere else.

note.source_type: Continuity of a Function at a Number
note.title: Continuity of a Function at a Number
note.heading: Continuity of a Function at a Number
note.paragraph: A function $$f$$ is continuous at a number $$x = a$$ if the following conditions are satisfied.

list.item: $$f(a)$$ is defined.
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)$$ exists.
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = f(a)$$

section.paragraph: Thus, a function $$f$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ if the limit of $$f$$ at $$x = a$$ exists and has the value $$f(a)$$ . Geometrically, $$f$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ if the proximity of $$x$$ to $$a$$ implies the proximity of $$f(x)$$ to $$f(a)$$ .
If $$f$$ is not continuous at $$x = a$$ , then $$f$$ is said to be discontinuous at $$x = a$$ . Also, $$f$$ is continuous on an interval if $$f$$ is continuous at every number in the interval.

Figure 40 depicts the graph of a continuous function on the interval $$(a,b)$$ . Notice that the graph of the function over the stated interval can be sketched without lifting one’s pencil from the paper.

example.heading: Solution

list.item: The function $$f$$ is continuous everywhere because the three conditions for continuity are satisfied for all values of $$x$$ .
The function $$g$$ is discontinuous at $$x = 2$$ because $$g$$ is not defined at that number. It is continuous everywhere else.

The function $$h$$ is discontinuous at $$x = 2$$ because the third condition for continuity is violated; the limit of $$h(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ exists and has the value $$4$$ , but this limit is not equal to $$h(2) = 1$$ . It is continuous for all other values of $$x$$ .
The function $$F$$ is continuous everywhere except at $$x = 0$$ , where the limit of $$F(x)$$ fails to exist as $$x$$ approaches zero (see Example 3a, Section 2.4).
Since the limit of $$G(x)$$ does not exist as $$x$$ approaches zero, we conclude that $$G$$ fails to be continuous at $$x = 0$$ . The function $$G$$ is continuous everywhere else.

section.heading: Properties of Continuous Functions
section.paragraph: The following properties of continuous functions follow directly from the definition of continuity and the corresponding properties of limits. They are stated without proof.

note.title: Properties of Continuous Functions
note.heading: Properties of Continuous Functions

list.item: 1. The constant function $$f(x) = c$$ is continuous everywhere.
2. The identity function $$f(x) = x$$ is continuous everywhere.

note.paragraph: If $$f$$ and $$g$$ are continuous at $$x = a$$ , then

list.item: 3. $$\left\lbrack f(x)\rbrack^{n} \right.$$ , where $$n$$ is a real number, is continuous at $$x = a$$ whenever it is defined at that number.
4. $$f \pm g$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ .
5. $$\mathit{fg}$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ .
6. $$f \slash g$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ provided that $$g(a) \neq 0$$ .

section.paragraph: Using these properties of continuous functions, we can prove the following results. (A proof is sketched in Exercise 101)

note.source_type: Continuity of Polynomial and Rational Functions
note.title: Continuity of Polynomial and Rational Functions
note.heading: Continuity of Polynomial and Rational Functions

list.item: A polynomial function $$y = P(x)$$ is continuous at every value of $$x$$ .
A rational function $$R(x) = p(x) \slash q(x)$$ is continuous at every value of $$x$$ where $$q(x) \neq 0$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the values of $$x$$ for which each function is continuous.
example.heading: Solution

list.item: The function $$f$$ is a polynomial function of degree $$3$$ , so $$f(x)$$ is continuous for all values of $$x$$ .

The function $$g$$ is a rational function. Observe that the denominator of $$g$$ —namely, $$x^{2} + 1$$ —is never equal to zero. Therefore, we conclude that $$g$$ is continuous for all values of $$x$$ .

The function $$h$$ is a rational function. In this case, however, the denominator of $$h$$ is equal to zero at $$x = 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ , which can be seen by factoring it. Thus, $$x^{2} - 3x + 2 = (x - 2)(x - 1)$$ We therefore conclude that $$h$$ is continuous everywhere except at $$x = 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ , where it is discontinuous.

section.paragraph: Up to this point, most of the applications we have discussed involved functions that are continuous everywhere. In Example 4, we consider an application from the field of educational psychology that involves a discontinuous function.

section.heading: Intermediate Value Theorem
section.paragraph: Let’s look again at our model of the motion of the maglev on a straight stretch of track. We know that the train cannot vanish at any instant of time and it cannot skip portions of the track and reappear someplace else. To put it another way, the train cannot occupy the positions $$s_{1}$$ and $$s_{2}$$ without at least, at some time, occupying an intermediate position (Figure 43).

section.paragraph: To illustrate the Intermediate Value Theorem, let’s look at the example involving the motion of the maglev again (see Figure 27). Notice that the initial position of the train is $$f(0) = 0$$ and the position at the end of its test run is $$f(10) = 400$$ . Furthermore, the function $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack 0,10\rbrack$$ . So the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that if we arbitrarily pick a number between $$0$$ and $$400$$ —say, $$100$$ —giving the position of the maglev, there must be a $$\overline{t}$$ (read “ $$t$$ bar”) between $$0$$ and $$10$$ at which time the train is at the position $$s = 100$$ . To find the value of $$\overline{t}$$ , we solve the equation $$f\left( \overline{t} \right) = s$$ , or
giving $$\overline{t} = 5$$ ( $$t$$ must lie between $$0$$ and $$10$$ ).

It is important to remember when we use Theorem 4 that the function $$f$$ must be continuous. The conclusion of the Intermediate Value Theorem may not hold if $$f$$ is not continuous (see Exercise 102).

The next theorem is an immediate consequence of the Intermediate Value Theorem. It not only tells us when a zero of a function $$f$$ [root of the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ ] exists but also provides the basis for a method of approximating it.

section.heading: 2.5. Concept Questions

list.item: 1. Explain what is meant by the statement $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}f(x) = 2$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}f(x) = 4$$ .

2. Suppose $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{-}}f(x) = 3$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1^{+}}f(x) = 4$$ . What can you say about $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}f(x)$$ ? Explain. What can you say about $$f(1)$$ ? Explain.
3. Explain what it means for a function $$f$$ to be continuous (a) at a number $$a$$ and (b) on an interval $$I$$ .

4. Suppose $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{-}}f(x) = L$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a^{+}}f(x) = M$$ , where $$L$$ and $$M$$ are real numbers. What conditions on $$L$$ , $$M$$ , and $$f(a)$$ will guarantee that $$f$$ is continuous at $$x = a$$ ?

5. Determine whether each function $$f$$ is continuous or discontinuous. Explain your answer. $$f(t)$$ gives the altitude of an airplane at time $$t$$ . $$f(t)$$ measures the total amount of rainfall at time $$t$$ at the Municipal Airport. $$f(s)$$ measures the fare as a function of the distance $$s$$ for taking a cab from Kennedy Airport to downtown Manhattan. $$f(t)$$ gives the interest rate charged by a financial institution at time $$t$$ .
6. Explain the Intermediate Value Theorem in your own words.

section.heading: Using Technology Finding the Points of Discontinuity of a Function
section.paragraph: You can very often recognize the points of discontinuity of a function $$f$$ by examining its graph. For example, Figure T1a shows the graph of $$f(x) = x \slash (x^{2} - 1)$$ obtained using a graphing utility. It is evident that $$f$$ is discontinuous at $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 1$$ . This observation is also borne out by the fact that both these points are not in the domain of $$f$$ .

section.paragraph: An examination of this graph does not reveal any points of discontinuity. However, if we factor both the numerator and the denominator of the rational expression, we see that
$$\begin{array}{l} {g(x) = \frac{(x + 1)(x - 2)(2x + 3)}{(x + 1)(x - 2)}} \\ {\phantom{g(x)} = 2x + 3} \end{array}$$
provided that $$x \neq - 1$$ and $$x \neq 2$$ , so its graph in fact looks like that shown in Figure T3.
